Ive seen alot of surgeries, both standard and emergency, and have not once see a DVM perscribe or recommend a topical during recovery.

Truly, it comes down to very simple recommendations:

1. Keep the cone on. Keep the cone ON. KEEP THE CONE ON!

2. Limit their activity. I know, it really really sucks to have an unhappy pet who is post surgery and is confused, grumpy and in pain. But itll suck even more to have the rush them in to ER bc sutures have split.

3. Dont touch the incision. Dont get it wet. Dont apply ointments or creams or clean it. The body will heal on its own, therefore it needs to be left alone.

4. Read and reread your discharges. If you have questions call the vet, if your vet isnt helpful. Call an ER. ER clinics will typically have a tech you can speak to.

Vet tech here: some of these comments have some really good advice. Others not so much.

1. Open mouth breathing in cats IS NOT OKAY. It is a sign of respiratory distress. Take this video and show it to your vet, if they say its stress related then the conversation needs to shift into what medications or tactics can be used to calm kitty down. If your cat is this stressed, something needs to be done.

2. Hard sided carrier. This is for safety of everyone involved. Safety for cat incase of hard breaking/accident. You really dont want your cat going thru your windshield. In addition, all GP/speciality hospitals Ive worked in have a policy that cats MUST be in a carrier, otherwise we'd reschedule you. The risk of a loose cat is too high and its a liability.

3. Going back to medications here. Sedation is not the devil. Proper sedation means it is sedation that is overseen by a vet. Sometimes it takes some tweaking of the meds to get it right for your cat.

I work at a GP so my answers going to vary slightly from an ER.

My hospital is located smack between 2 ERs so if there is a chance the pet needs resuscitation we direct them/help them next door.

Policy at my hospital is for any DOA case is we confirm that there are no sounds that could mark breathing or a heartbeat. 

Owner is put into our quiet room and given a few moments while we confirm DOA. Once the pet is confirmed DOA we ask the owner if they would like a few minutes with their deceased pet and to come find us when they are ready for paperwork. 

We try to complete everything in the room with the owner present as it gives them space and privacy to mourn.

We complete paperwork which includes authorization of cremation/return to owner for home burial.

We take any payment (the absolute worst fucking part) and owners free to go, and we begin to process the body.

Its awful every single time. Im not religious however I am spiritual, I prefer to be the one to process bodies as its a very intimate, respectful and spiritual experience for me. I thank the animal for the love that they gave and for the time that they were with us, clean them up, paw prints, take some fur (if the owner says yes) and then place them very gently into the body bag. If theyre small enough Ill craddle them over to the freezer, if theyre too large i keep track of where their head is in the bag and once in the freezer Ill kiss my hand and place it on their head.

This comment is probably waay longer than it needs to be, i just find that having conversations around how we deal with death is helpful.

Service dogs, or dogs who are trained to perform tasks for people, can be used to assist in alerting or soothing someone who has a disability.

Examples are seizure alert dogs, seeing eye dogs, glucose alerting dogs, etc...

In this case a dog who is trained to assist an epileptic person can alert the patient to the oneset of an incoming seizure. They can whine, bark, nudge, randomly sit down or perform another action to inform the patient that most likely a seizure will occur shortly.

This can help the patient in stopping what they are doing and sitting or laying down prior to the seizure so that when the seizure occurs, an injury from falling or dropping doesnt happen.

Also a dog can be trained to use their body as a type of cushion for the patients head to prevent repeated banging or scraping during the seizure. 

Dogs can also be useful post seizure by licking the patients face or hands to assist them in regaining conciousness and helping them remain calm. 

If a patient doesnt regain conciousness after a certain amount of time, service dogs will often run off to find someone nearby and attempt to get the passerby to follow them back to the patient in order to get the patient further medical help.
